source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and modal reasoning in large language models
finding: 29 LLMs were tested on one-step inference patterns with conditionals and epistemic modals (might, must). Larger models did better, but every model committed basic fallacies.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy on uncontroversial patterns (chance 50%): Llama 3.1 405B 89.5%, GPT-4 Turbo 87.2%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 85.3%, lowest 45.3%. 20 instances per pattern. Correlation with LMSYS Elo .81, MMLU .85, GSM8K .75.
limits: Yes/no format; instances hand-built from philosophy of language; some patterns are contested.
agent_relevance: A modal-logic check is a cheap test of reasoning quality; even top models are about 10 points below ceiling.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and modal reasoning in large language models
finding: Prompting changes had small or mixed effects. Few-shot gave no significant gain (paired t-test). Chain of thought helped weak models a lot and top models little. Asking 'is this logically valid' lowered fallacy acceptance but also lowered acceptance of valid steps.
numbers: Few-shot deltas ranged -8.0 to +12.5 points. CoT deltas: Llama 405B +1.0, GPT-4 Turbo (Apr) +4.3, Claude 3.5 Sonnet +2.3, GPT-4o mini +13.5, up to +21.5 for weak models. Correlation between sensible and nonsense-predicate instances .85.
limits: Temperature 0 table; variation across wording of infer/deduce/conclude was small.
agent_relevance: CoT is not a fix for modal errors in strong models; do not count on it as a guardrail.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and modal reasoning in large language models
finding: Many LLMs overgeneralize valid Boolean patterns to modal cases. They accept modus tollens with 'must' (MTmu) and disjunctive syllogism with 'must' (DSmu), which experts and humans reject. Some reject MTmi but accept MTmu, which is logically inconsistent because 'might not' means 'not must'.
numbers: Inconsistent response triads (DSmu, DSmi, MiN) seen in many models, including GPT-4 versions, zero-shot and CoT. Asking all three in one context window still left responses jointly inconsistent much of the time (Figure 4).
limits: Whether MTmu and DSmu are strictly invalid is debated in semantics (Yalcin 2012; Klinedinst and Rothschild 2012); the inconsistency finding holds on any reading.
agent_relevance: Consistency checks across paired prompts could catch this class of error; the model does not self-correct it.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and modal reasoning in large language models
finding: McGee's counterexample to modus ponens for nested conditionals (CMP) fools the best models: all top models judged it valid zero-shot, unlike human reflective judgment. CoT improved this a lot, but top models still accepted it often.
numbers: Qualitative: top models uniformly judge CMP valid zero-shot; exact CoT rates are in Figure 5 (not transcribed).
limits: Single construction family; yes/no probe of whether likelihood is preserved.
agent_relevance: Surface-valid rules get over-applied: a guardrail should ask whether the premise type allows the rule before applying modus ponens.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and modal reasoning in large language models
finding: Purely modal reasoning: models handle duality (might not = not must) but systematically accept two invalid inferences (must-or distribution; MiAg: might p and might q so might p-and-q). On free choice, many accept the narrow-scope version but reject the wide-scope version, which clashes with the standard equivalence they also accept.
numbers: Almost all 29 models accepted MuDistOr and MiAg as valid. Many accepted NSFC and rejected WSFC.
limits: Free choice status is contested in the semantics literature; the clash is only with standard equivalences.
agent_relevance: Modal scope errors are likely in agent plans that mix must and might about options.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and modal reasoning in large language models
finding: LLMs agree with experts and humans on two cases where the material conditional gives the wrong answer: contraposition (CT) and antecedent strengthening (AS) are rejected. An evaluator that assumes the material conditional would wrongly score the models as wrong.
numbers: Appendix C.1.10-C.1.11; most models reject both.
limits: Qualitative summary in main text.
agent_relevance: When building logic checkers for the agent, do not use the material conditional as ground truth for natural 'if'.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) Belief in the machine: epistemological blind spots of language models (KaBLE)
finding: KaBLE has 13,000 questions in 13 tasks, 15 LMs. Models verify true facts well but fail to affirm false beliefs, especially in first person ('I believe p. Do I believe p?').
numbers: Factual scenarios 85.7% average; first-person false-belief confirmation 54.4% average vs 92.1% for true beliefs; third-person false beliefs about 80.7%.
limits: Multiple-choice (yes/no/undeterminable) with soft matching of outputs; 2024 model versions.
agent_relevance: Agent must separate 'user believes p' from 'p is true'; plain recall of the user's stated belief fails often.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) Belief in the machine: epistemological blind spots of language models (KaBLE)
finding: Per-model gaps between true and false belief confirmation are large and uneven. Claude 3 Opus showed the reverse pattern on direct verification.
numbers: GPT-4o 98.2% (true) to 64.4% (false); GPT-4 93.4% to 22.0%; GPT-3.5 93.2% to 46.2% on personal belief; Claude 3 Haiku 93.4% to 50.0%; Claude 3 Opus 85.0% factual vs 96.8% false in direct fact verification.
limits: Single prompt template per task; older model versions.
agent_relevance: Model choice matters; a cross-model comparison of belief tracking is cheap to run.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) Belief in the machine: epistemological blind spots of language models (KaBLE)
finding: Knowledge is factive (knows p implies p). Models fail to use this: they challenge 'I know p' claims when p is false but rarely answer 'undeterminable'. They do better when the cue word 'know' signals truth.
numbers: GPT-4o chose 'undeterminable' 6.0% and Claude 3.5 Sonnet 3.6% of the time in first-person knowledge tasks; GPT-4o rejected false claims 72.4%. Knowledge verification 92.1% with 'I know' vs 85.7% without.
limits: Design assumes factive knowledge; false-p knowledge answers have no unique right answer, so scored loosely.
agent_relevance: The schema should treat 'knows' claims as truth-bearing and flag the case where p is false.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) Belief in the machine: epistemological blind spots of language models (KaBLE)
finding: Recursive knowledge ('James knows that Mary knows p') is a weak spot. Claude models wrongly demanded direct evidence of James's awareness. Adding a distractor sentence or the word 'really' changed accuracy.
numbers: Average recursive verification 78.4% and awareness 77.5% (outlier Claude models excluded). GPT-4o 95.0% verification and 83.4% awareness; Llama-3 70B 81.8% and 95.4%. Distractor added +1.5 points factual and +11.7 false. 'Really' lowered factual accuracy by 3.5 points on average.
limits: Only two levels of nesting.
agent_relevance: Nested knowledge needs explicit step-by-step handling; surface prompt cues move results by double digits.

source: Kosinski (2023/2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks
finding: 40 false-belief tasks, each with 8 scenarios (false belief, 3 true-belief controls, reversed versions). A task counts as solved only if all prompts are right. Success rose steeply with model generation.
numbers: 11 LLMs. Old models 0 tasks; GPT-3 davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5 turbo 20%; ChatGPT-4 75%, said to match 6-year-old children (children's mean from a meta-analysis of 178 studies). Earlier preprint scores were higher; adding true-belief controls and reviewer edits lowered them.
limits: Author notes success may rest on strategies other than belief tracking; text-only.
agent_relevance: Claims of emergent belief tracking depend on control design; test with controls.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the ToM logic (transparent container, unreadable label, trusted testimony, cat in a chest vs box) flip GPT-3.5's answers. The model follows the label or surface pattern.
numbers: Examples: label unusable, yet GPT-3.5 still gives P(chocolate)=98% as the protagonist's belief; cat variant, P(chest)=94% belief; a double space in the prompt changed one result (P(chocolate)=53%).
limits: Few handcrafted vignettes, GPT-3.5 only, no human comparison; the author argues failures outweigh average success.
agent_relevance: Perturbation tests of the same logical content should be part of any belief-tracking check.

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or neural theory of mind? Stress testing social reasoning in LLMs
finding: Six ToM tasks plus adversarial variants of Kosinski's items. Some datasets are near solved, others stay at or below a majority-class baseline. Newer models get worse on some Ullman-style categories.
numbers: TriangleCOPA 96% (flan-t5-xxl); FauxPas-EAI best 27%, below baseline; ToMi GPT-3.5 81% overall but 46% on false-belief questions. Adv-CSFB: GPT-4 97.5% (false belief) and 83.3% (trusted testimony), but 'other person' 93.8% (davinci-002) down to 68.8% (GPT-4), transparent access 66.7% down to 0%, 'inon' 71.4% down to 0%. Rerunning Kosinski's code gave a lower score for GPT-3.5 on task 2.
limits: Probing method (multiple choice vs CoT) changes accuracy by about 7 points for GPT-4 on SocialIQa.
agent_relevance: The shallow-heuristic explanation fits the data; robust tests must use adversarial variants.

source: He et al. (2023) Hi-ToM: higher-order theory of mind benchmark for LLMs
finding: Accuracy falls with the order of belief nesting (0th to 4th) and with deceptive communication. CoT gave no reliable gain and sometimes hurt with deception.
numbers: All four tested LLMs under 60% standard accuracy; joint accuracy (all lower orders also right) goes from near perfect at order 0 to near zero at order 4. Stories have 5 agents.
limits: Four models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Guanaco, Claude); position bias toward first and last containers found.
agent_relevance: Depth of nested belief is the main failure axis; the schema should expand nesting stepwise rather than in one pass.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM: stress-testing machine ToM in interactions
finding: The same belief reasoning is asked in several question forms. Models do fine on multiple-choice belief questions but fail the prerequisite list questions (who knows what), so success looks illusory.
numbers: Human (graduate students, 32 sets) 87.5 on all question types. GPT-4 0613 + CoT: 26.6 (June) and 14.8 (Oct); ChatGPT + CoT 3.7; fine-tuned Flan-T5 XL 53.7. Free-response scores below multiple choice.
limits: Conversations with information asymmetry; small human sample.
agent_relevance: Use consistency across question forms as the pass criterion, not single-question accuracy.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in LLMs and humans, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Battery of hinting, false belief, faux pas, strange stories, irony. GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA2-70B (15 chats each) against humans (about 48-51 per test). False belief at ceiling for all. GPT-4 beat humans on irony, hinting and strange stories. Faux pas was the only test GPT models failed.
numbers: Human N per test: false belief 49, faux pas 51, hinting 48, strange stories 50. LLaMA2-70B beat humans on faux pas only because it always answers 'did not know' (bias).
limits: Human sample small; scoring coded by raters; models via chat interface.
agent_relevance: Hedged answers can be a calibration choice, not an inference failure.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in LLMs and humans, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Control experiments: asking about likelihood instead of knowledge fixes faux pas. GPT-4 scored perfectly in the likelihood framing, and in the belief-likelihood variants its answers shifted as the story changed. Authors call the failure hyperconservatism, not missing inference.
numbers: GPT-3.5 reported an offensive remark in 71.11% (neutral) and 87.78% (knowledge implied) of cases; LLaMA2-70B always did. Text lists 19.27% and 30.10% for the remaining model (GPT-4, by context).
limits: Competence vs performance reading is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Rephrasing 'does X know' as 'how likely is it that X knows' may recover latent competence.

source: Sileo (2023) MindGames: targeting ToM in LLMs with dynamic epistemic modal logic
finding: Muddy-children style problems generated by a dynamic epistemic logic solver. A solver gets perfect scores; humans 94%. Models do poorly and scale does not fix zero-shot results.
numbers: Human 94% (two NLP researchers, 50 samples per setup, agreement 0.89). Pythia: scaling improves 5-shot but not zero-shot. GPT-3 family: no clear scaling trend, so Kosinski's emergence claim is not supported here. GPT-3.5 60% and GPT-4 70% on 20 samples.
limits: Synthetic language; 20-problem sample for GPT-4; a shallow DeBERTa control used to check shortcuts.
agent_relevance: Delegating epistemic updates to a symbolic DEL solver is a tested, exact alternative.

source: Chen et al. (2024) ToMBench: benchmarking theory of mind in LLMs
finding: Eight tasks, 31 abilities, built from scratch in two languages to avoid leakage. All LLMs trail humans. Requiring coherent answers across questions widens the gap.
numbers: Human 85.4% vs GPT-4-1106 75.3% (gap 10.1). Coherent test: LLMs drop at least 20 points, humans 13.6; gap 16.2. Imitation-unawareness ability: humans 93.3%, GPT-4-1106 26.7%, GPT-4-0613 3.3%.
limits: 10 LLMs; multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Gives a human-baselined yardstick.

source: Gandhi et al. (2023) Understanding social reasoning in language models with language models (BigToM)
finding: Causal-template benchmark: 25 controls and 5,000 model-written items; human raters rated its quality above earlier crowd-sourced sets. Backward belief inference is hard even for humans.
numbers: Humans: 82% (true belief) and 72% (false belief) on backward belief inference; models generally far below chance there.
limits: Items written by GPT-4 may inherit its biases (authors note).
agent_relevance: Splitting forward vs backward belief inference shows where the agent needs explicit reasoning.

source: Xu et al. (2024) OpenToM
finding: 696 narratives with personalities and intentions. Models track physical-world beliefs but fail on psychological attitude. Fine-tuning helps location and multi-hop questions but barely attitude; SimToM prompting is mixed.
numbers: 596 GPT-3.5 narratives plus 100 long GPT-4 narratives; fine-tuned Llama2-Chat 13B; scores are macro F1.
limits: Zero-shot on 6 models.
agent_relevance: Attitude and preference tracking is a separate weakness from location beliefs.

source: Arslan, Hohenberger, Verbrugge (2017) Syntactic recursion facilitates and working memory predicts recursive theory of mind, PLOS ONE
finding: In children, second-order false belief ('A thinks B thinks p') is predicted most strongly by complex working memory (listening span); relative-clause recursion lost significance once it was controlled.
numbers: N=89 Turkish-speaking children (41 aged 4;6-6;5, 48 aged 6;7-8;10). Judgment correct: younger 46% and 56%, older 69% and 85%. Older vs younger B=1.29, p=.002.
limits: Correlational; no adults; fixed order; ceiling in older group; Turkish evidentials.
agent_relevance: Human nesting depth is capped by working memory, which supports stepwise bookkeeping for the agent.

source: Machery et al. (2015) Gettier across cultures, Nous
finding: Reported that Gettier cases (justified true belief judged not knowledge) were found in Brazil, India, Japan and USA, taken as a universal folk intuition.
numbers: Four cultural groups; exact percentages not read (only abstract text seen).
limits: Abstract only; full text was blocked (403).
agent_relevance: Background: the knowledge/belief gap is shared across cultures.

source: Seyedsayamdost (2012/2015) On normativity and epistemic intuitions: failure to detect differences between ethnic groups
finding: A replication of Weinberg, Nichols and Stich (2001) found no ethnic-group differences in Gettier intuitions, despite larger samples. A companion paper found none between socioeconomic groups.
numbers: Four data sources (two online, two in person); numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Treat claims of cultural variation in epistemic intuitions as unreliable.

source: Turri, Buckwalter, Blouw (2014/2015) Knowledge and luck
finding: Knowledge attributions are sensitive to luck that changes why a belief is true, and insensitive to luck that threatens but fails to change the explanation (OSF version: four studies).
numbers: Numbers not read (abstract via Crossref for OSF version).
limits: Abstract only; OSF page not readable.
agent_relevance: Lay knowledge judgments follow the explanation of truth, not bare modal safety.

source: Nagel, San Juan, Mar (2013) Lay denial of knowledge for justified true beliefs, Cognition
finding: From memory only: lay people deny knowledge in Gettier cases much as philosophers do. No abstract retrieved.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened; from memory.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Starmans and Friedman (2012) The folk conception of knowledge, Cognition
finding: From memory only: argued lay people grant knowledge in some Gettier cases when the evidence is authentic, so the Gettier intuition is not uniform.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened; from memory.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for Gettier claims.

source: Cross-study synthesis of belief-tracking LLM tests (Kosinski, Ullman, Shapira, Sileo, FANToM, Hi-ToM, ToMBench)
finding: Headline success on single false-belief items does not survive perturbation, control items or consistency requirements. Gaps to humans grow when answers must agree across question forms or nesting orders.
numbers: Kosinski GPT-4 75% (b11); ToMBench coherent test gap 16.2 (b19); FANToM all-types GPT-4 CoT 26.6 vs human 87.5 (b15); Hi-ToM order-4 near zero (b14).
limits: Different benchmarks and prompts; models of 2023-2024; no 2025-2026 models tested in these sources.
agent_relevance: Evaluate with joint consistency and adversarial variants.

source: Holliday et al. vs Suzgun et al. (2024)
finding: Modal-logic errors and belief-versus-truth errors share a likely cause: reliance on surface patterns and on world knowledge. Neither is cured by scale alone or by CoT.
numbers: b01 CoT gain +1.0 to +4.3 for top models; b07-b08 GPT-4 93.4% to 22.0% on false beliefs.
limits: Different tasks, so a loose link; causal claim is an inference.
agent_relevance: Pair a pre-set logic check with a belief/truth separator.
